subtype: Hunger and sleep turn into tantrums [Actor]
passage:
"No! Blue cup!" Pranav flings the red cup and howls.
"It's the same milk," says Vasudha Didi, picking it up.
"NO!" He flops on the floor, kicking.
Amma glances at the clock. "Lunch is late. He's hungry, and he skipped his nap."
"So it's not the cup?" Vasudha asks.
"It's the tummy."
Amma sets down a plate of warm dal-rice. Pranav eats, hiccuping. Soon he is asleep on the mat, one hand on the red cup.

qa.q: What does Amma set down for Pranav?
qa.a: A plate of warm dal-rice.

qa.q: Why is Pranav so upset about the cup?
qa.a: He is hungry and tired after skipping his nap, so he feels cranky and overwhelmed, and a small thing like the cup sets him off.

qa.q: Which choice calmed Pranav, and why?
qa.a: Serving lunch instead of arguing about the cup; once his hunger and tiredness were met, the tantrum faded.

qa.q: How does Vasudha see the tantrum at first?
qa.a: Vasudha thinks it is about the cup, since the milk is the same, and learns from Amma that it is really about his tummy.

grounding: A hungry, overtired toddler melts down over a cup until a meal and sleep settle him, while his sister learns why.

subtype: Teacher notices a child cannot focus before snack [Observer]
passage:
On Children's Day the rehearsal for the class dance ran forty minutes over, and snack time kept slipping. Sunaina Miss noticed Anirban first. He couldn't stay in his spot. He tugged his collar, kicked a chair leg, and when a friend bumped him, he burst into tears.
Another teacher muttered, "He's being naughty today."
Sunaina wasn't so sure. She checked the clock and remembered his mother saying he had left without breakfast. She sat him down with his tiffin, idli and chutney. Ten minutes later he was humming, legs swinging, calm.

qa.q: What was in Anirban's tiffin?
qa.a: Idli and chutney.

qa.q: What was Sunaina Miss thinking when another teacher called Anirban naughty?
qa.a: She felt doubtful, suspecting hunger rather than naughtiness, since snack was late and he had left without breakfast.

qa.q: What small step helped, and why?
qa.a: Sitting Anirban down with his tiffin; his tears and fidgeting came from hunger, so food calmed him faster than a scolding would have.

qa.q: What was the late morning like for Anirban?
qa.a: For Anirban, hungry and kept standing, it was uncomfortable and upsetting, so a small bump felt huge until he ate.

grounding: A teacher sees a hungry child fidgety and tearful before a late snack, and calm once he has eaten.

passage:
Monday of Navratri week. The puja ran late, and Uday ran for the bus without breakfast. In maths, Ma'am drew fractions on the board. Uday saw only a round paratha cut into quarters. His stomach growled so loudly that Arohi giggled.
Wednesday. The same rush, the same empty stomach. Ma'am asked him what three-quarters meant. He stared at the board. All he could think about was the samosa smell drifting from the canteen.
Friday. Maa pressed a roll of roti and jaggery into his hand at the door, and he ate it on the bus. In maths he got the fraction question right and even explained it to Arohi.

qa.q: What did Maa give Uday on Friday?
qa.a: A roll of roti and jaggery.

qa.q: What was on Uday's mind in Wednesday's maths class?
qa.a: He felt hungry and restless, so distracted he could think only of the samosa smell from the canteen instead of three-quarters.

qa.q: What changed on Friday, and what does it suggest for busy school mornings?
qa.a: Uday ate on the bus, so his mind was free for maths; even quick food on a rushed morning can help a child follow lessons.

qa.q: How might Arohi see Uday across the week?
qa.a: Arohi giggles at his growling stomach on Monday, but by Friday he is explaining fractions to her, which may surprise her.

grounding: A schoolchild who skips breakfast can think only of food in class, until eating frees his attention.

subtype: Sleep loss changes mood and choices [Actor]
passage:
Monday, first rains. Sonali had watched episodes till 3 a.m., the rain drumming on the tin roof. In class, when Charu borrowed her sharpener without asking, Sonali snapped, "Can't you get your own?" Charu's eyes widened.
Thursday. Another 2 a.m. night, no breakfast. When the dance captain said her step was off, Sonali left the team group in a huff, then cried in the washroom, feeling low and stupid.
The next Monday. After a week of the phone on Mumma's dresser from ten and poha before school, the world felt less sharp. Sonali found Charu at the gate. "Sorry about the sharpener. And I've asked to rejoin the dance group. I was a mess."
Charu grinned. "You were a zombie."

qa.q: Where did the phone stay at night during the better week?
qa.a: On Mumma's dresser, from ten.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling when she cried in the washroom on Thursday?
qa.a: She felt low and stupid, embarrassed at leaving the group in a huff after too little sleep and no breakfast.

qa.q: What changed Sonali's mood, and what could she keep doing?
qa.a: Putting the phone away at ten and eating poha before school; keeping steady sleep and meals would protect her mood and her choices.

qa.q: How might Charu have felt when Sonali snapped about the sharpener?
qa.a: Charu was likely surprised and a little hurt, her eyes widening at Sonali's sudden sharpness.

grounding: A teenager's late nights make her irritable and rash, until steady sleep and breakfast settle her mood.

passage:
Guru Nanak Jayanti, 11:30 pm
The gurdwara across the road is lit up, and the smell of langar drifted in all evening, and I ate nothing but four cups of hostel tea and a packet of biscuits. Three nights of four hours' sleep. Today Leela asked, just asked, if I wanted to revise thermodynamics together, and I told her she only wants my notes. Her face.
Then at 6 pm I emailed Prof. Menon asking to drop the elective, mid-semester, because one quiz went badly. Sent it without even reading it back.
Now, lying here, both feel like someone else did them. Leela left a langar parcel on my desk anyway, with a note: "Rashmi, EAT." I'm going to eat it, sleep properly, and apologise to her first thing.

qa.q: What did Rashmi email Prof. Menon about?
qa.a: Asking to drop the elective, mid-semester, because one quiz went badly.

qa.q: How does Rashmi feel lying in bed that night?
qa.a: Rashmi feels regretful and ashamed, as if someone else had snapped at Leela and sent the email.

qa.q: What should Rashmi do before making any more big choices?
qa.a: Eat, sleep properly and wait a day; Rashmi could ask Prof. Menon to hold the request and talk it over once rested.

qa.q: How might Leela feel after being told she only wants Rashmi's notes?
qa.a: Leela was likely hurt, yet still left a langar parcel and a note, which shows she cares despite the sting.

grounding: A student living on tea and little sleep snaps at a friend and makes a rash choice before exams, then regrets both.

subtype: Long scarcity leaves little room for planning [Observer]
passage:
Valentina had been a caseworker at the Madrid drop-in centre for a year when she met Kofi. He was twenty-four, sleeping in a different hostel every week and working night shifts at a loading bay. Three times she gave him the form for the evening electrician course. Three times it came back blank.
A colleague sighed. "He just isn't motivated."
Valentina had watched him nod off mid-sentence, eat the centre's sandwiches fast, keep his bag strapped on even while sitting. She didn't think it was laziness. There was simply no room left in his days for next year.
In March the centre found him a stable room and a day shift. Two weeks later Kofi walked in with the form filled out, and a question about night classes.

qa.q: How many times did Kofi's form come back blank?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What did Valentina feel when the colleague called Kofi unmotivated?
qa.a: She felt doubtful of that view and concerned for Kofi, sensing he was exhausted and scraping by rather than lazy.

qa.q: What made the difference for Kofi, and what does it suggest?
qa.a: A stable room and a day shift; once the basics were secure he had room to plan, so help with basics can come before expecting long-term plans.

qa.q: What was life like for Kofi before March?
qa.a: Kofi was tired and on guard, moving hostels every week, working nights and keeping his bag on, so the future had to wait.

grounding: A caseworker sees that a young man's blank forms come from scarcity, not laziness, and that stable basics free his mind.

passage: On Baisakhi last year everybody went to the fair, but I stayed on the verandah with the cardboard boxes. I, Amandeep, was building a gurdwara with a dome made from half a ball. I cut little arches with Mummy's scissors and glued toothpicks for the railings. When Kunal came back with his balloon, it was dark, and I hadn't even noticed the lights come on. "You missed the giant wheel!" he said. I didn't mind at all. There was no prize, no competition, nothing. I just wanted to see if the dome would stay up. It did.

qa.q: What did Amandeep use for the dome?
qa.a: Half a ball.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel about missing the giant wheel?
qa.a: Amandeep didn't mind at all, feeling happy and absorbed, more curious about whether the dome would stay up than about the fair.

qa.q: How could the family encourage this kind of absorption?
qa.a: Give Amandeep time, boxes and glue, and ask about the building itself rather than offering prizes or turning it into a contest.

qa.q: What might Kunal have thought on coming back from the fair?
qa.a: Kunal was probably surprised that Amandeep had sat on the verandah till dark building a model instead of riding the giant wheel.

grounding: A child is lost for hours building a cardboard model, forgetting time and caring nothing for prizes.

passage:
The Navratri golu dolls were up in every house on the street, and it was pouring when Lakshmi tucked her notebook of kritis into a plastic bag and set off for her Carnatic class. The bus stop was flooded; a twenty-minute walk lay ahead.
At the corner, Ritu and two others were sharing an umbrella and a video. "Going for your paati music again?" Ritu called. The others laughed.
Lakshmi's ears went warm. She had heard it all term: old-people songs, boring. She kept walking, humming the tricky sangati she had practised all week.
In class, when she finally got it right, her teacher nodded once. Lakshmi felt something settle inside, like a key turning in the right lock. Wet socks and all, this was hers.

qa.q: How long was the walk to the Carnatic class?
qa.a: A twenty-minute walk.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel when Ritu called out, and what kept her going?
qa.a: Her ears went warm with embarrassment, but her own love of the music, the sense that it was truly hers, mattered more than fitting in.

qa.q: What could Lakshmi say if the teasing continues?
qa.a: Something calm and honest, like "I just love it," and keep going; she might even invite Ritu to hear her sing at a golu.

qa.q: How might Ritu see Lakshmi's music?
qa.a: Ritu sees it as old-fashioned paati music and may not realise how much it means to Lakshmi, or that the joke stings.

grounding: A teenager keeps going to classical music class in the rain despite classmates' jokes, because it feels true to her.

passage:
Monday, 26 December. The offer email came at noon: the famous consulting firm, a salary three times what anyone in Tenzin's family had earned. Hafsa screamed and hugged Tenzin in the library corridor. Amala cried on the phone, proud.
Wednesday. The call with the small group that builds science labs in mountain schools ran an hour over. Tenzin asked question after question about the kids in Ladakh, forgetting to be nervous, face lit up.
New Year's Eve. On the hostel roof beside Hafsa, Tenzin typed the reply to the firm, "Thank you, but I must decline," and pressed send with shaking hands. Fireworks went up over the city.
"Scared?" Hafsa asked.
"Terrified," Tenzin said. "And weirdly calm. Like my shoes finally fit."

qa.q: What did Tenzin type in the reply to the firm?
qa.a: "Thank you, but I must decline."

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel after pressing send?
qa.a: Tenzin felt terrified and weirdly calm at once, like shoes that finally fit, because the lab work matched what Tenzin cared about.

qa.q: What helped Tenzin choose, and what could someone in a similar spot do?
qa.a: Noticing how the lab call brought Tenzin alive; a person could compare how each option feels in practice and talk it over with someone trusted, like Hafsa.

qa.q: How might Amala feel about Tenzin's decision?
qa.a: Amala, who cried with pride at the offer, might feel worried or disappointed at first and need time to see why the other path fits Tenzin better.

grounding: A young adult turns down a famous, high-paying job for values-fitting work and feels both fear and calm.

passage:
Mentor log, college robotics lab, Thursday. Sarika
Ishita stayed till nine again tonight. Nobody asked her to; the project marks were submitted last week. She was rebuilding the gripper arm for the third time, just to see if a softer grip could pick up a tomato without squashing it. When it finally worked she laughed out loud, alone in the lab, then photographed the tomato from four angles.
Her father called me last month asking if she should do an MBA like her cousin. I didn't push either way. Today I gave her a spare key card, the old 3D printer nobody uses, and a login for the lab's parts cupboard. Told her: "Break things. Tell me what you learn."
Plan: check in every two weeks, and otherwise keep out of her way.

qa.q: What was Ishita trying to pick up with the gripper arm?
qa.a: A tomato, without squashing it.

qa.q: What does Sarika seem to feel watching Ishita stay late?
qa.a: Sarika seems pleased and respectful, seeing a genuine interest that isn't about marks and wanting to protect it.

qa.q: Why might tools and space work better than steering Ishita toward a set career?
qa.a: The key card and printer let her follow her own curiosity, which feeds her growth; pushing an MBA path could crush the very thing that makes her light up.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel on receiving the key card and the printer?
qa.a: Ishita would likely feel trusted and excited, free to keep experimenting on her own terms.

grounding: A mentor notices a student lighting up and staying late for her own interest, and gives her tools and space.
